paper: A proof of Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture

tree.label: A proof of Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture

children.label: Title
children.text: A proof of Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture — OpenAI.

children.label: Abstract
children.text: We prove that every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many vertices at directed distance two as at directed distance one, resolving Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture positively.

children.label: §1 heading
children.text: Section 1 — Introduction.

children.label: Definition: oriented graph
children.text: An *oriented graph* is a finite directed graph with no loops, no multiple arcs, and no pair of opposite arcs. Its underlying undirected graph need not be complete or connected.

children.label: Definition: $N_1^+(v)$, $N_2^+(v)$ + the conjecture
children.text: $$N_1^+(v)=\{u:v\to u\},\quad N_2^+(v)=\{w\notin\{v\}\cup N_1^+(v):\exists u,\,v\to u\to w\}.$$ $N_2^+(v)$ = vertices at directed distance exactly two, counted once. Seymour's conjecture: some vertex has $|N_1^+(v)|\le|N_2^+(v)|$.

children.label: Theorem 1.1 (main result)
children.text: Every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex $v$ such that $$|N_1^+(v)|\le|N_2^+(v)|.$$

children.label: Remark: sinks, essential content
children.text: Resolves the conjecture with no connectivity or degree hypothesis; a sink already satisfies it. Removing vertices reached in one step is essential to the assertion.

children.label: Preview of §5 (weighted) and §6 (cycles)
children.text: The theorem yields the vertex- and arc-weighted forms via Seacrest's equivalences (two quantifier orders), stated in §5, and short-directed-cycle consequences in §6 (e.g. min in/outdegree $\ge n/3$ forces a directed triangle).

children.label: Background: tournament case & history
children.text: Conjecture recorded by Dean & Latka; tournament case (Dean's conjecture) proved by Fisher via Farkas, combinatorially by Havet & Thomassé; extensions by Fidler–Yuster, Ghazal, and others.

children.label: Background: degree/ratio & random results
children.text: Degree-condition and ratio results (Kaneko–Locke, Chen–Shen–Yuster, Huang–Peng), random-orientation results, and dense-case preprints.

children.label: What this proof builds on
children.text: Builds on the minimal-counterexample and graph-product methods of Brantner–Brockman–Kay–Snively and Seacrest's subset perspective; adapts Seacrest's Lemma 4 edge-deletion idea. Main new ingredient: a pruning bound for finite binary relations whose deletion cost depends on points left uncovered.

children.label: “Proof strategy.”
children.text: Paragraph heading: Proof strategy.

children.label: Image operator $F_D$
children.text: $F_D(S)=\{y:\exists x\in S,\,x\to y\}$, $F_D^2=F_D\circ F_D$; $F_D$ does not subtract $S$. In an oriented graph $N_2^+(v)=F_D^2(\{v\})\setminus F_D(\{v\})$.

children.label: Step A — counterexample ⟶ strict subset inequality
children.text: Minimum-order then minimum-arc counterexample; arc deletion gives $|F_D^2(S)\setminus F_D(S)|<|F_D(S)\setminus S|$ for nonempty proper $S$; a transitive-tournament blowup turns this into $|U|+|F_G^2(U)|<2|F_G(U)|$, all indegrees positive. (§2.)

children.label: Step B — the extremal obstruction
children.text: Two diagonal-containing families of pairs in $V(G)\times V(G)$ maximizing $M+d$; complementing second iterated images yields prospective families of combined size $>M+2d$.

children.label: Step C — pruning restores compatibility
children.text: The pruning lemma (§3) restores compatibility, keeps the diagonal, deletes $\le d+d'$ members, making the objective $>M+d$ — the contradiction (§4).

children.label: How the pruning lemma is proved
children.text: Bounds a matching in an augmented bipartite graph; opposite-order coordinate changes factor one matrix through two index sets, and a maximum-rank choice makes kernels control matching size. Independent of orientation.

children.label: §2 heading
children.text: Section 2 — From a counterexample to a strict subset inequality.

children.label: Section intro: the operator $F=F_D$
children.text: Convert a counterexample into a graph whose first image exceeds the average of a set and its second image. Here $F=F_D$ is the union of out-neighborhoods in base graph $D$; $F(S)$ need not be disjoint from $S$.

children.label: Prop 2.1 (Counterexample reduction)
children.text: If Theorem 1.1 has a counterexample, there is a finite nonempty oriented graph $G$ with every vertex of positive indegree and $$|U|+|F_G^2(U)|<2|F_G(U)|\quad(\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V(G)).$$

children.label: Two-step plan
children.text: Two steps: minimality gives a strict deficit for subsets of a counterexample; a transitive-tournament blowup turns that deficit into the required inequality.

children.label: Relation to Seacrest's Lemma 4
children.text: The arc-deletion argument adapts Seacrest's Lemma 4 (his $\lambda=1$ gives $|F^2(S)\setminus F(S)|<|F(S)|$ in an edge-minimal counterexample). Lemma 2.2 strengthens the right side to $|F(S)\setminus S|$ under minimum order then minimum arcs.

children.label: Lemma 2.2 (Subset deficit)
children.text: Let $D$ be finite nonempty oriented with $|N_1^+(v)|>|N_2^+(v)|$ for all $v$; pick $D$ of minimum order then minimum arcs. Then $D$ is strongly connected, all indegrees positive, and $$|F^2(S)\setminus F(S)|<|F(S)\setminus S|\quad(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V(D)).$$

children.label: Strongly connected, no sink
children.text: A sink satisfies the inequality, so $D$ has no sink and $>1$ vertex. A terminal strong component would be a smaller counterexample; so $D$ is strongly connected and every vertex has an in-neighbor.

children.label: Fix $S$; define $I$, $E$, $g$
children.text: $I=F(S)\cap S$, $E=F(S)\setminus S$, $g(T)=|F(T)\setminus(I\cup T)|$. Strong connectivity gives $E\ne\varnothing$. Grow $T$ from $\varnothing$ to $E$ so each step raises $g$ by less than the vertices added.

children.label: Delete arcs $S\to E\setminus T$; find $v\in S$
children.text: $D_T$ deletes all arcs $S\to E\setminus T$. Arc-minimality gives $v$ with $|N^+_{1,D_T}(v)|\le|N^+_{2,D_T}(v)|$; it must have lost a first out-neighbor, so $v\in S$ and $Q=F(\{v\})\cap(E\setminus T)\ne\varnothing$.

children.label: Where surviving 2-paths land
children.text: In $D_T$, $F^2_{D_T}(\{v\})\subseteq I\cup T\cup F(T)$; any newly counted second out-neighbor lies in $Q\cap F(T)$.

children.label: The lost second out-neighbors $C$
children.text: $C=F(Q)\setminus(I\cup T\cup Q\cup F(T))\subseteq N^+_{2,D}(v)$ (using $v\notin F(Q)$ by orientation), and no vertex of $C$ survives in $D_T$.

children.label: Deficit increment is $<|Q|$
children.text: With $d_2<d_1$: $g(T\cup Q)-g(T)=|C|-|Q\cap F(T)|\le |Q|+d_2-d_1<|Q|.$

children.label: Sum over the growth to $T=E$
children.text: Summing gives $g(E)<|E|$; since $F^2(S)\setminus F(S)=F(E)\setminus(I\cup E)$ has size $g(E)$, the deficit follows.

children.label: Bridge: amplifying the integer deficit
children.text: Each unit of base deficit contributes a full block; internal contribution costs $\le1$ per base vertex. Construction: the lexicographic product $D[T_m]$ (as in Brantner–Brockman–Kay–Snively Thm 4.3), but estimated for every nonempty proper subset.

children.label: Lemma 2.3 (Transitive-tournament blowup)
children.text: Replace each vertex of $D$ (positive indegrees, satisfying the subset deficit) by a transitive tournament on $m>n$ vertices, with all arcs between blocks of an arc. The result $G$ is oriented, has positive indegrees, and satisfies $|U|+|F_G^2(U)|<2|F_G(U)|$.

children.label: Internal block estimates
children.text: Label blocks $1..m$ (small→large). For least element $a$, $f(T)=\{a+1,..,m\}$, so $|T|-|f(T)|\le1$, $f^2(T)\subseteq f(T)$, $|T|-2|f(T)|+|f^2(T)|\le1$. $G$ is oriented with positive indegrees.

children.label: Support $S$, $H_0$, and $|F_G(U)|$
children.text: $T_v$ = labels of $U$ in block $v$, $S=\{v:T_v\ne\varnothing\}$, $H_0=F(S)\cup F^2(S)$. Every $F(S)$-block is filled: $|F_G(U)|=m|F(S)|+\sum_{v\in S\setminus F(S)}|f(T_v)|$.

children.label: Bounding $|F_G^2(U)|$
children.text: 2-paths with two external arcs land in $F^2(S)$-blocks; one external arc in $F(S)$-blocks; internal-only give $f^2(T_v)$. So $|F_G^2(U)|\le m|H_0|+\sum_{v\in S\setminus H_0}|f^2(T_v)|$.

children.label: Combine: $\le -m+n<0$ for proper $S$
children.text: $|U|-2|F_G(U)|+|F_G^2(U)|\le m(|F^2(S)\setminus F(S)|-|F(S)\setminus S|)+n$. For $S\subsetneq V(D)$ the deficit makes the bracket $<0$, so the bound is $\le -m+n<0$.

children.label: The case $S=V(D)$
children.text: Positive indegrees give $F_G(U)=F_G^2(U)=V(G)$, so $|U|-2|F_G(U)|+|F_G^2(U)|=|U|-|V(G)|<0$ since $U$ is proper.

children.label: Proof of Prop 2.1 (combines 2.2 & 2.3)
children.text: Choose a counterexample of minimum order then minimum arcs; Lemma 2.2 supplies positive indegrees and the subset deficit, and Lemma 2.3 (any $m>|V(D)|$) supplies $G$.

children.label: §3 heading
children.text: Section 3 — Pruning two families of pairs.

children.label: Section intro: the deletion bound
children.text: A deletion bound for two families of ordered pairs, charging deleted members to original conflicts plus post-deletion uncovered points. Holds for every finite binary relation; no orientation needed.

children.label: Lemma 3.1 (Pruning)
children.text: For finite $X$ with relation $\to$ and $\mathcal R,\mathcal C\subseteq X\times X$: $(p,j),(i,s)$ *conflict* if $p\to i$, $s\to j$. With $Z=\{(i,j)\}$, $H=\{(p,s)\}$ over conflicts, there are conflict-free $\mathcal R'\subseteq\mathcal R$, $\mathcal C'\subseteq\mathcal C$ keeping every conflict-free member with $$|\mathcal R\setminus\mathcal R'|+|\mathcal C\setminus\mathcal C'|\le|H|+|\{z\in Z\text{ uncovered}\}|.$$

children.label: Toward the proof: a rank fact
children.text: The proof bounds a matching in an augmented bipartite graph via matrix ranks; first the elementary rank fact (Lemma 3.2). A matrix supported on $T$ has zero entries outside $T$.

children.label: Lemma 3.2 (Kernels at maximum support rank)
children.text: For finite $I,J$, $T\subseteq I\times J$: if $D:\mathbb R^J\to\mathbb R^I$ has maximum rank among matrices supported on $T$, then for $x\in\ker D$, $y\in\ker D^{\mathsf T}$, $(s,j)\in T$, $x_jy_s=0$.

children.label: Trivial case & conventions
children.text: No conflicts ⟹ retain everything, $Z=H=\varnothing$. Coordinate bases throughout; empty minors have determinant 1.

children.label: Part 1 — augmented graph & the matching bound
Build $\Gamma$
children.text: Bipartite $\Gamma$: parts $\mathcal R\sqcup Z_L$, $\mathcal C\sqcup Z_R$. Join conflicting members; join each member to the opposite $Z$-copy it covers. Conflict-free members are isolated.

children.label: Figure: one conflict ⟶ 3-edge path
children.text: A conflict between $r=(p,j)$, $c=(i,s)$ forces path $z_L-c-r-z_R$, $z=(i,j)\in Z$; copies $z_L,z_R$ distinct. Conflicts can share vertices/edges.

children.label: A small cover gives the charge $|H|+q$
children.text: A vertex cover $K$ of size $\le|Z|+|H|$ omitting isolated vertices: deleting its original members leaves no conflict, and $|K\cap(\mathcal R\sqcup\mathcal C)|\le|H|+q$ with $q$ post-deletion uncovered $Z$-points.

children.label: Part 2 — decompose a maximum matching
children.text: Maximum matching $\mathcal M$ with fewest original–original edges ($k$); $\alpha$ ($\mathcal R$–$Z_R$), $\beta$ ($Z_L$–$\mathcal C$), $\ell=|\alpha|$, $t=|\beta|$, $|\mathcal M|=k+\ell+t$. Augmenting paths show $\alpha,\beta$ are each maximum in their subgraph.

children.label: Part 3 — four maps, one commuting square
children.text: Variables $a_{xy},b_{xy}$ give $L,N,B,A$ with $NL=AB$. Goal: an assignment with $\rank L=\ell$, $\rank N=t$, $\dim\ker A\ge k$, forcing $|\mathcal M|\le|Z|+|H|$ via rank–nullity.

children.label: Part 4a — simultaneous generic choice
children.text: Via Edmonds' generic-rank/matching correspondence: pick coefficients so $\alpha$'s columns base $\im L$, $\beta$'s base $\im N^{\mathsf T}$, and each $D^{p,i}$ has maximum support rank — one product of nonzero polynomials, nonzero at some real assignment.

children.label: Part 4b — kernel restriction gives $\dim\ker A\ge k$
children.text: Lift matched endpoints to $u^r\in\ker L$, $v^c\in\ker N^{\mathsf T}$; Lemma 3.2 gives $u_{pj}v_{is}=0$ per conflict, so $Bu^r$ are independent and $A(Bu^r)=NLu^r=0$; thus $|\mathcal M|=k+\ell+t\le|Z|+|H|$.

children.label: Part 4c — matching bound ⟶ cover (König)
children.text: Alternating-path cover $K=(\mathcal V_L\setminus W_L)\cup W_R$ covers every edge, $|K|=|\mathcal M|\le|Z|+|H|$, omits isolated vertices; the charge inequality proves the lemma.

children.label: §4 heading
children.text: Section 4 — The extremal contradiction.

children.label: Section intro
children.text: Use the pruning lemma to rule out the graph from Prop 2.1, converting the strict subset inequalities into a strict increase of an extremal quantity on two families of pairs.

children.label: Prop 4.1 (no such graph)
children.text: There is no nonempty finite oriented graph $G$ with every vertex having an in-neighbor and $$|U|+|F^2(U)|<2|F(U)|\quad(\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V(G)).$$

children.label: Coordinate operators & compatibility
children.text: $F_1S$ advances the first coordinate along an arc, $F_2S$ the second. $P,Q$ *compatible* if $F_1P\cap F_2Q=\varnothing$ (= no conflict). $P=Q=\Delta$ is compatible by orientation.

children.label: The maximized objective $M+d$
children.text: Among compatible pairs with $\Delta\subseteq P\cap Q$, maximize $M+d$ where $M=|P|+|Q|$, $d=|X|^2-|F_1P|-|F_2Q|$ = uncovered points. A maximum exists since $X$ is finite.

children.label: Columns/rows proper ⟶ sum the hypothesis
children.text: Each column $P_j\ni j$ and row $Q_i\ni i$ is proper (else compatibility breaks). Summing the concavity inequality: $|P|+|F_1^2P|<2|F_1P|$ and $|Q|+|F_2^2Q|<2|F_2Q|$.

children.label: Complement families gain $>M+2d$
children.text: $\mathcal R=(X\times X)\setminus F_2^2Q$, $\mathcal C=(X\times X)\setminus F_1^2P$ give $|\mathcal R|+|\mathcal C|=2|X|^2-|F_2^2Q|-|F_1^2P|>M+2d$. They may conflict.

children.label: The diagonal survives and is conflict-free
children.text: $\Delta\subseteq\mathcal R\cap\mathcal C$, and each diagonal member is conflict-free (a conflict would force $(i,s)\in F_1^2P$ or $(p,j)\in F_2^2Q$). So pruning's preservation clause applies.

children.label: The conflict set $H$: $|H|\le d$
children.text: For a conflict, $(p,s)\in F_1P$ or $F_2Q$ would force membership contradictions; so $H\subseteq(X\times X)\setminus(F_1P\cup F_2Q)$ and $|H|\le d$.

children.label: Apply pruning; the $M+d$ contradiction
children.text: Pruning gives conflict-free $P'\subseteq\mathcal R$, $Q'\subseteq\mathcal C\supseteq\Delta$, so $\le d+d'$ deletions and $|P'|+|Q'|+d'>M+2d-(d+d')+d'=M+d$ — contradicting maximality of $(P,Q)$.

children.label: Proof of Theorem 1.1
children.text: If the theorem were false, Prop 2.1 produces a nonempty finite oriented graph with positive indegrees satisfying the concavity inequality; Prop 4.1 rules it out.

children.label: §5 heading
children.text: Section 5 — Weighted consequences.

children.label: Section intro
children.text: Applies Theorem 1.1 through Seacrest's established equivalences; the equivalences are not new here.

children.label: Corollary 5.1 (weighted forms)
children.text: For a nonempty finite oriented graph $D$: (i) for every $\eta\ge0$ some $v$ has $\eta(N_1^+(v))\le\eta(N_2^+(v))$; (ii) a total-mass-one weighting (not all positive) works for every $v$; (iii) for every arc weighting $w\ge0$ some $v$ has $\sum_s\beta_v^w(s)\ge\sum_{u\in N_1^+(v)}w(vu)$.

children.label: (iii) = Seacrest's arc-weighted form
children.text: Seacrest's Prop 2: his arc-weighted conjecture is equivalent to the unweighted one, so Theorem 1.1 gives (iii).

children.label: (i) by specializing $w(us)=\eta(s)$
children.text: Setting $w(us)=\eta(s)$ makes $\beta_v^w(s)=\eta(s)$ on $N_2^+(v)$ and $0$ elsewhere, so (iii)'s two sides become $\eta(N_2^+(v))$ and $\eta(N_1^+(v))$.

children.label: (ii) via Farkas on $M_D$
children.text: $M_D$ has $\pm1$ on second/first out-neighbors; reversing arcs transposes it. Seacrest's Farkas-lemma Theorem 1 gives a nonzero $\eta\ge0$ with $M_D\eta\ge0$ (the alternative contradicts (i) on $\overleftarrow D$); normalize.

children.label: §6 heading
children.text: Section 6 — Directed-cycle consequences.

children.label: Section intro
children.text: In a triangle-free oriented graph every exact second out-neighbor is a non-neighbor; combined with Theorem 1.1 this gives degree and order bounds (Thomassé/Sullivan, Behzad–Chartrand–Wall).

children.label: Corollary 6.1 (non-neighbors & cycles)
children.text: For order-$n$ oriented $D$ with $Z(v)=V\setminus(\{v\}\cup N_1^+(v)\cup N_1^-(v))$: (i) no directed 3-cycle ⟹ some $v$ has $d^+(v)\le|Z(v)|$, $n-1\ge2d^+(v)+d^-(v)$; (ii) $\delta^+,\delta^-\ge n/3$ ⟹ a directed 3-cycle; (iii) $r$-regular with girth exactly four ⟹ $n\ge3r+1$.

children.label: $N_2^+(v)\subseteq Z(v)$ & part (i)
children.text: No directed 3-cycle ⟹ a second out-neighbor is not $v$, a first out-neighbor, or an in-neighbor, so $N_2^+(v)\subseteq Z(v)$. Theorem 1.1: $d^+(v)\le|Z(v)|$; with $n-1=d^++d^-+|Z|$ gives (i).

children.label: Parts (ii) and (iii)
children.text: (ii): triangle-freeness would give $n-1\ge2\delta^++\delta^-\ge n$. (iii): girth four excludes 3-cycles and the regular count gives $n-1\ge3r$.
